passage.title: The Picture and the Person
paras: Some photographs change the world. A single image of a child fleeing danger can do what a thousand reports cannot: it can make people stop, feel and act. Charities raise money because of such pictures; governments are pressed to change their policies.

But every photograph of suffering has a person in it, and that person did not choose to be seen at the worst moment of their life. They may never know where their image travels. Their family may see it on a stranger's phone. Their grief may become someone else's headline, or worse, someone else's entertainment.

Editors must decide quickly, and the pressure to publish first is strong. Some argue that the truth must always be shown, however painful. Others argue that dignity matters more than clicks. Both have a point.

A photograph of suffering should be published only if it serves the people in it: if it tells their truth, protects their dignity and asks something of us. Otherwise it is not journalism. It is just looking.

questions.q: Summarise one argument for publishing and one against, in your own words.
questions.a: For: images reveal truth and can move people to act. Against: they can take away dignity without consent.

questions.q: Explain the effect of the final short sentence.
questions.a: 'It is just looking.' is blunt and short; it condemns careless publishing.
